# Education in Norway: Key Overview
Education in Norway is composed of three main stages: elementary school (barneskole, ages 6–12), lower secondary school (ungdomsskole, ages 13–16), and upper secondary school (videregående skole, ages 16–19). Elementary and lower secondary are compulsory, forming the 'grunnskole' (foundation school). The curriculum covers diverse subjects, including mathematics, languages, science, social studies, and religion, which is taught from a pluralistic perspective. Students receive grades starting in lower secondary, which impact admission to upper secondary schools. Upper secondary education offers both general and vocational tracks, and since the 1994 reform, students can switch between paths without losing all accumulated credits. Vocational programmes typically utilize a 2+2 model: two years of school followed by two years of apprenticeship. The education system employs various grading scales, with final diplomas based on both continuous assessment and random subject exams.
Higher education in Norway requires a general university admissions certificate, usually obtained via completion of general upper secondary studies or through adult alternative routes. State-run universities and university colleges offer bachelor's (3 years), master's (5 years), and PhD (typically 8 years) programs. Private institutions exist but are few; 10% of higher education students attend them. Most higher education is public and quality-assured by NOKUT. Special education is largely integrated within ordinary schools, with robust support from educational psychologists and social welfare specialists. The school year runs August–June, with generous vacations and national holidays. Notably, Norway provides for camp schools as part of primary and secondary education, mandates inclusivity in public and private schooling, and supports an academic calendar with two semesters per year.
